paragraphs.text: One thing that, in the Scriptures, God is said to be is “the Father of compassions, and God of all encouragement” (2 Corinthians 1: 3), and I want to speak very simply of the kind of encouragement that God gives, especially at critical times. He would love to use a season like this to encourage us, because of the peculiarly momentous times in which we are; I speak of this in a positive sense. There is the side of crisis. That word has perhaps been too much in our minds, a fact which would maybe emerge from a realisation on our part that with God there are no crises. He has His hand on everything. What a comfort that is! We may have come to a particular point in church history where the reality of decline is brought home to us, in every sphere coming under our notice, save the sphere of God’s operations in grace and in power.

The Spirit of God would remind us of the imminence of what is final. What is final involves that the divine triumph over every adverse thing is to be asserted. Before God brings finality in He allows things to ripen, to disclose what they really are. If it is what we speak of as the great ecclesiastical system and the error that marks it, God brings it to a point where it is manifest. God is doing that in very many ways, but He would have us very close to Himself, and very sensitive as to what His heart is in such days as these; because His heart is not changed, His ideals are not changed. The Man whom He exalted is still the Man whom He has exalted. The place of power in which He has set Christ is still His place. He is the One of whom Scripture speaks that He has the power to subdue all things to Himself (Philippians 3: 21). It is not that He shall have, He has the power to do that. How wonderful it is to see Christ up there and to get the constantly stabilising touch to the soul of realising that He is established in pre-eminence; God has established Him in pre-eminence. The knowledge of that is in these hearts of ours.

And yet, rather like Elijah, I fear we sometimes become discouraged. God would say, ‘Do not look to circumstances for your encouragement; do not look to conditions in man’s world for encouragement. Look to Me for encouragement’. He delights to afford it. Elijah was very low, and I suppose that has been in the experience of all of us here at some time or in some circumstance. Things seemed very low. He “came and sat down under a certain broom-bush, and requested for himself that he might die”. What an outlook! Is this, in any sense at all, the outlook of any one of us here? It might not perhaps be in the full extent of what is conveyed in Elijah’s words, but is it in our minds, if I may use the expression, just to fade out? God would remind us that He has called us into His greatest things. He has not just suggested or imparted to us a knowledge of certain things, He has called us into His things. Scripture speaks of His calling us “into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord”, 1 Corinthians 1: 9. That fellowship stands related to Christ personally in that gloriously dignified title, “his Son”, God’s Son; yet at the same time His immediate relation to ourselves, “our Lord”, is in view, and that is to govern the fellowship.

How are we in the fellowship? Is it a kind of positional matter with us? Is it just a question of where we go for meetings, and such like? What is our realisation of the real power of the fellowship of God’s Son, Jesus Christ our Lord? God has called us to that. He has not given us an option to find our part in it, He has called us into it. How are we answering to the call? It becomes increasingly precious, increasingly strengthening to us in such times as these, to find our part in life and in divine support in what belongs to the fellowship of God’s Son.

But to revert to Elijah, he was thoroughly discouraged. The circumstances were such that if he was occupied with them he might well be discouraged. The outward circumstances today are such that, from that viewpoint, we might well be, God would say, I will encourage you. Do not look elsewhere for your encouragement; He will give you the encouragement. Elijah said, “It is enough—now, Jehovah, take my life; for I am not better than my fathers”. Things are beginning to come out. He says he is not better than his fathers. Why should he seek to be? He is thinking of himself. How often we get turned in upon ourselves! God would say as we turn that way, ‘You will not find any encouragement there’. Here is a man who wants to be better than his fathers. Why should he be so? What does he want to be?
But then what happens? “An angel touched him, and said to him, Arise, eat!” He needs food. God has agencies under His hand just to bring in what is needed in the way of food.

One of the most vital things to strengthen us against discouragement is food. Where is our food? It is in Jesus, it is in Christ. It may be food for the wilderness, the Manna, as the type presents it; or it may be food for the land. Christ glorified in a sphere to which He fitly belongs, food that relates to the heavenly situation, the old corn of the land. Get your eye on Christ and feed, the Spirit of God would say. Let the light and glory of that Person really enter your soul, attracting you as it must, but becoming nourishment to you. Get a view of Jesus, not as He was (glorious as that was) but as He is, a view of Christ, the mighty Victor, the supreme One. He is not yet manifested in His supremacy, though soon to be so manifested, but He has immediately the power to subdue all things to Himself.

What Elijah sees at his head is “a cake, baked on hot stones, and a cruse of water”. That is, he has not only food, but refreshment. And what refreshment there is in the appreciation of Christ! What refreshment is to be known in the upsurge of the Spirit of God in your soul to make much of Christ, a living spring in yourself attaching your heart to Jesus where He is, and bringing right into you what relates to Himself. It is a cake baked on hot stones; prepared food, fresh food. It is not something that you have tasted before, stale through neglect, but the freshness of all that is in Christ; that is to become nourishment to persons who may be discouraged. What provision God has made for the very needs in detail of the pathway in which those who love Him are! “And he ate and drank, and lay down again”. This is an amazing happening, but he lay down again. God sometimes does test us out as to our deeper roots. Are we easily

discouraged, dear brethren? God would bring us right to the root to show us what the prime interests really are; the whole situation really is that Christ is supreme. He is about to come in the assertion of His rights. Everything here is being exposed in its true character as contrary to Him and contrary to divine thoughts, in view of His coming to take up His rights. But our portion is in Him and with Him where He is. Could there be any greater basis of encouragement than that? You belong to Christ; you belong to the scene in which the glory of Christ is shining; as to the testimony here you belong to the fellowship into which God has called you, which is abundantly furnished with every resource for its supply and sustaining until He come.

Elijah lies down again. It points to something which is very real in many of our experiences; for a time, maybe, we give earnest attention, and yet perhaps we still flag. We lie down again. But is God displaying anger with His servant? “The angel of Jehovah came again the second time, and touched him, and said, Arise, eat; for the journey is too great for thee”. The angel is adding something this time, “The journey is too great for thee”, as if he would say, ‘It is a matter of urgency that you get fully nourished and prove the support that God shall give’. Let there be no looking to oneself for support. The word is, It is too great for you. Who of us could fill out in any strength of his own any part in the testimony related to God’s glorious Son? Maybe we have been trying to; perhaps that is how the discouragement came in. You are not on the journey on the basis that the supply is to come from you. God has called you into His matters on the basis that the supply is with Him, especially in the Spirit, and the supply

is entirely adequate. But you must feed. You must appropriate all that God has established in Christ. Find for yourself, in your own experience, not only the love of Christ, but the power He has to come into your soul and to strengthen and stimulate you as He does it. Get a view of Christ and see how He is in full charge of every circumstance in the testimony here; as being so He has charged Himself to see you through, as you are committed to His testimony, because the thing is too great for yourself anyway.

It says of Elijah, “And he arose, and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb the mount of God”—a fine destination, a getting back to God’s prime thoughts. I suppose Horeb would stand for the divine thoughts in their full, glorious, original character, not modified by human thoughts nor adjusted in their balance by human ideas, but the divine thoughts just as they really are. He is getting back to the excellence of what is in the mind and heart of God for those who love Him, a place with Christ, a place in the glory, and a place in regard of the prime position of the assembly as with Christ ultimately in the exercise of His headship. Let us feed on these things, dear brethren. How much the Spirit of God has given us to instruct us in them. Maybe the instruction has entered our minds, but has it commanded our hearts? That, perhaps, is the point for us today, the place that Christ has as dwelling in our hearts by faith.

Elijah goes on this long journey; forty days and forty nights, in the strength of that food. He has learnt a lesson. It is not in his own strength, it is in the strength of that food that he goes. What an experience for Elijah! He

still has a certain way to go. The Spirit of God is going along with this man. He wants him thoroughly settled. God’s encouragement is like that. He wants us thoroughly settled, not to be encouraged today and discouraged tomorrow, not to be flagging today and urgent tomorrow. He would have us steady in divine strengthening to pursue what may need to be pursued.

So Jehovah says to him, “What doest thou here. Elijah?”. Maybe that question is one that the Spirit of God would raise with each of us today. ‘What doest thou here?’. He is seeking to establish what is really in Elijah’s soul as to where he is, not necessarily to condemn him, “What doest thou here, Elijah?” The prophet is to be brought into the realisation that he is in relation with God—that God has called him into His matters, and is abundantly supplying him with food, food that it would seem he had never tasted before. He stands in relation to God. God has proved from His side how He stands in relation to His servant in abundance of supply; but now how does the servant stand in relation to God?

Have we taken up matters responsibly for God in His interests? Am I in the local meeting that way? Do I undertake my daily duties that way, as having Christ’s interests as my prime interest? Have we an understanding with God as to that? “What doest thou here, Elijah?”. Why are you here? What are you doing? What is your objective? Poor Elijah! “I have been very jealous for Jehovah the God of hosts”. Self-occupation is a most tenacious thing; it is something that the Spirit of God would help us to meet by engaging us with Christ, and sustaining our engagement with Christ; yet He comes in in grace, in the firmness of His own word, just to challenge the situation.

So the blessed God takes in grace a certain course of instruction with His servant. He is caused to see certain very impressive things, and each of them is covered by the simple statement that God was not in it. God is not acting that way. There were certain lines of action, ways of acting in the assembly, alas, in which we had our part, and alas it would seem that they are still current. God would say to us, I am not in that; that is not the way; He is applying Himself to matters in this time in grace. Elijah hears “a soft gentle voice”. That is, God is still speaking; He is still conveying things, still making known His mind, yea, and insisting on His mind too. “A soft gentle voice”—Oh, the grace in this, beloved brethren, that gives us to see how God is working from His side. That would dispel human thoughts, human ideas, entrenched thoughts that may have come, not from God, but from man.

“A soft gentle voice. And it came to pass when Elijah heard it, that he wrapped his face in his mantle, and went out, and stood in the entrance of the cave”. That, I believe, is a critical point in a positive sense, “He wrapped his face in his mantle”. He was, having to do with God. His eyes were not to see God. He was in a right fear of God, and even for us in this time of grace, beloved brethren, there is a right fear of God, a recognition that God has His rights in matters; the matters are indeed His matters, and no one of us is to trifle with His matters or under-rate them in any sense. It seems as if Elijah comes to that, and the word again comes, “What doest thou here, Elijah?”. He is still clinging to the same statement, still saying the same thing. It is to show us, I believe, that God is going on and He will not have us stand in His way. He is going on very patiently, but in His patience He is insisting upon His on rights, the rights of Christ, the rights of the Spirit.

So eventually Jehovah says to him, “Go, return on thy way”. He gives directions, clear directions, directions that have in mind that the testimony is to continue. Thank God, Elijah’s later course would show that God wrought wonderfully yet in this man. But even when Elijah is still saying the same thing about himself, God breaks in, and tells him that he is to go forward and do this, and this, and this, including the anointing of one to whom he was to pass this touch of prophetic power in due time. The testimony is to go on, and God is saying to Elijah, ‘I have brought you into this and I am insistent that you continue in it’. And He adds, “I have left myself seven thousand in Israel, all the knees that have not bowed unto Baal, and every mouth that hath not kissed him”. What a disclosure—seven thousand! God makes such disclosures to us, as to the real value of what He has. He delights to disclose it for the encouragement of true hearts that may for the time have become over-occupied with the negatives, over-occupied with themselves; this is a baneful thing, prevalent in the history of a good many of us. God would say, Your encouragement is to be from Me.

The testimony is going on, and God has in that testimony what fitly belongs to Him in the pursuit of it, and He is going to carry it through irrespective of us. Yet how much He has invested in this man in the patience of His way to bring him fully into matters, the matters that are to go on to the finish. Let us think about it that way, beloved brethren. How much God has lavished in

gracious supply upon us to have us fully with Him in what He is doing. He would assure us that what He is doing is going through to completion, but He would search our hearts, stimulate our affections, and encourage us, that we might go right through until the Lord comes—divinely fitted, divinely nourished, divinely supplied, and if need be divinely awakened to the true greatness of the whole situation as it is according to God. May He help us in this, for His name’s sake.

articles.title: “I WORK A WORK IN YOUR DAYS”
articles.author: A. A. Bellamy

paragraphs.text: “The word of Jehovah”, it says, “was rare in those days”. I believe the Lord has challenged us, beloved brethren, about this, and I simply wish to encourage our hearts as to the verity of His word and His Spirit remaining among us. Conditions publicly could hardly have been lower than they were at this point in the first book of Samuel, yet, despite the rarity of the word and the infrequency of the vision, both the word and the vision took place, and at least there was one, and no doubt there were others, who received it. The official and responsible side is evidently in failure, and there is much that is negative in the whole public situation, but a feature of great encouragement, dear brethren, is that the lamp of God had not yet gone out. That, I believe, brings home to our hearts the urgency of the moment; the assembly is about to be translated and the lamp of God has not yet gone out. It is a moment of opportunity, calling upon us for greater dedication than we have ever known to the interests of Christ. Minding earthly things and seeking our own things belongs to the will of the nations, and the time past is sufficient for that; the rest of our time is to be for God’s will (see 1 Peter 4: 2).

God is addressing His word here to a young person. We are often reminded in these occasions that one generation passes away and another generation comes. What a generation Samuel represents!—fruit of assembly exercises, in sorrow and in the presence of the adversary—experiences not unknown to us. The boy Samuel stands out as the fruit of that. He is a man child (1 Samuel 1: 11) and he can accept responsibility immediately. The lamp of God not yet having gone out has also a bearing upon us in regard to our responsibility concerning the Spirit of God, and whether we at any time would have to say that our lamps are going out. It is a matter increasingly, beloved brethren, of our links with the Spirit, and of having oil in our vessels. We should be holding forth the word of life and appearing as lights in the world in testimonial effectiveness, fruit of our links with the Spirit not only individually but assembly-wise. On that line the lamp of God has not yet gone out.

Now the communication is personal here. One would long that this occasion might afford the Lord an opportunity to speak to some young person amongst us, indeed to us all, as He has often spoken. I wonder if we have heard a voice from the unseen world, in soul history with God, such as Mr. Darby refers to—
What powerful, mighty Voice, so near,
Calls me from earth apart—
Reaches with tones so still, so clear,
From th’unseen world my heart?

If any one has ever heard such a voice, beloved brother and sister, let it not be in vain. “Jehovah came, and stood, and called as at the other times”, and that at a time when the word of Jehovah was rare and a vision was not frequent. Think of the resources that there are at this time in the presence of the Spirit in the assembly. So the communication was to an individual, a word of appeal, like the Lord’s word, “Youth”, He says, “Wake up”, Luke 7: 14. He would call us all, out of a dead condition into a living state of things, to have a part in this great spiritual system which is for our help, our sustenance, and is to empower us increasingly in the service of God.

Now another feature is that God is, saying He will “do a thing in Israel”. I do not pretend to say what He is going to do, beloved brethren, but I think I have the sense that He is going to do something “at which both the ears of every one that heareth it shall tingle”. Are we ready for that—not only for the word and the vision, but for what God is going to do?

Then in Habakkuk, in a wider sphere, “See ye among the nations, and behold, and wonder marvellously; for I work a work in your days, which ye will not believe, though it be declared to you”. The nations are not out of God’s mind, surely not. He has visited them to call out of them a people for His name, and He says here that He will work a work among the nations. It is a question of what He is going to do, and what He is going to work. May the Lord grant us to be ready for it, for His name’s sake.

It says in Genesis 49: 28, “All these are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father spoke to them; and he blessed them—every one according to his blessing he blessed them”. Jacob is a father and he is blessing his sons, I suppose it would be right to say, in love (such becomes a father, and fatherly affection), but also with prophetic power. We have been speaking about prophecy and what is prophetic. There is no doubt that this father blessed his sons as a father, and a father should be able to bless, but he blesses with prophetic power. What it must have meant to Jacob to go back all these years, as he begins with Reuben and what Reuben had done, and then goes on to Simeon and Levi, remembering what they had done. So he goes on, and at the end it says this is the blessing with which he blessed them. With his knowledge of God and formation in himself in the mind of God, the truth as from God, he blesses them. It seems as if it must have been somewhat of a burden to him because in the midst of it he turns aside from addressing his sons, to address God. “I wait for thy salvation, O Jehovah”.

We should all bear in mind that there have been other fathers, maybe our own natural fathers in many cases, in the spirit of blessing and yet withal with a measure of prophetic power, who have gone over their history, and our histories, in the light of what is suitable to God, and have known something of the burden of carrying these things; but they have found their resource in it all in the prospect of God’s salvation. Maybe some of you younger brethren have more time left than others of us who are here. I would commend this to you, that there are those who are in the secret of God’s mind, who bear affection for you, but bear also the charge as to what is pleasing to the Lord and what is pleasing to God, and think of you and pray for you in affection, but having regard for what is due to Christ and what is due to the Father. I would make an appeal on this line that your history may not become an occasion of burden to such as may be spiritual fathers and who carry things for God and are sustained in so doing as Jacob was when he burst out, turning from them to God, “I wait for thy salvation”—‘I need Your help’.

I have read about the Son of God in John 17, for that is who is the theme in this chapter. It begins, as we so often delight in it, “These things Jesus spoke, and lifted up his eyes to heaven and said, Father …”. The Son of God is bringing before the Father those that He had with Him. How much He can say of them that is positive! All, we would now say, of course, is due to His own precious sacrifice of Himself, and to what has succeeded that in the coming of the Spirit, giving them power to answer to the truth. When He was here He kept them, He guarded them. It is a wonderful thing that He had kept those men, one of whom in the inscrutability of divine wisdom was the son of perdition. Perhaps we learn something about that in our times and our own history. Not that there was another—there was just one who was the son of perdition.

But the Son’s time here is coming to its end, and He is bringing His own before His Father. How much He is able to say of them; how much He is able to look forward to their being with Him where He is. That is anticipated—where He was, no doubt, in His spirit, but where He is now actually, and He anticipates their being with Him where He is to behold His glory which the Father had given to Him, that unique glory that is His as having accomplished all the Father’s will. But in the midst of it He says, “And now I come to thee”. How glorious it is!—a Man speaking to God the Father and saying “I come to thee”. All the Father’s will accomplished (in anticipation), His eternal purpose and pleasure secured, and persons who were the fruit of that work—we might say a sample—brought forward as He speaks to the Father. ‘Here they are—these are a sample’, because He can also speak of “those who believe on me through their word” (John 17: 20). How wide that is! How blessed it is that, in spite of all our failures as the sons of Jacob, that which God had in mind He is going to have. Thank God, He is having it already in some measure. May He have it more! Do not let the younger brethren put it off, because there is no time to lose. May He have it in all of us for the rest of our time.

Paul, in the last scripture, is finishing in spiritual vigour. Possibly anticipating imminent martyrdom, he is confident in God and Christ Jesus, “who is about to judge living and dead”, and in His appearing and His kingdom. Evidently not expecting to remain much longer, these things are in Paul’s mind and heart. As to himself he says, “I am already being poured out”. Such was the little time he had left. He was being poured out. How good it would be if you and I could be a little more on that line of being poured out. We know how much we are addicted to self-pleasing, and self-consideration, but Paul’s last days were spent like this—“already being poured out”. He is looking forward. “Henceforth”, he says, “the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will render to me in that day; but not only to me, but also to all who love his appearing”. Well, we should be among such, beloved brethren. May it be so, until He comes, for His name’s sake.

Christ is shining as the light of the morning, like the rising of the sun, and His shining is available for all. God has crowned Him with glory and honour and He is available to help us to understand that God is waiting to bless. It is one of the great results of the true light that we begin to understand that God wants to bless us. The darkness that Satan brings about would make us think that God is waiting to judge. The glorious truth is that God is waiting to bless. Christ is shining as the light of the morning and as the sunshine after the rain. God is not preparing to bring in rain today; the rain has already come. In the flood (Genesis 7) the rain came for forty days and forty nights, and the only persons who lived were those in the ark. The rain came down until all the mountains under all the heavens were covered. Jesus went into the greatest depths we could ever think of. All the floods came upon Him. There was darkness without parallel. When we speak today of the light of the morning, let us remember that there was a time when Jesus was in darkness. What darkness that was when He hung on the cross of Golgotha! There would be no good news for men if Jesus had not been into the darkness.

The true light began to shine when Jesus came into this world, but men did not want light. You and I do not want the light, according to what we are in the flesh; we shrink from it. We would rather keep in the darkness where, we think, God cannot see us; but let us remember that God sees us wherever we are. However young we are or however old, God knows all about us, and it is the God who knows all about us and our sins who sent His Son as Saviour of the world. When Jesus was here moving about amongst man He was here to bring light into every dark corner. The devil was always in retreat. Lepers were cleansed and the blind were caused to see, dead persons were raised, broken-hearted persons were healed, captives were brought into deliverance. There were men who had groaned under the bondage of Satan for, many a year, but when the light of God’s glorious Son shone upon, them the power of the enemy had to flee, as with the man who was found “sitting, clothed and sensible, at the feet of Jesus”, Luke 8: 35. He had spent a long time in the darkness of the tombs, but found his place in restfulness at the feet of the One who was the light of the world.

One woman had spent all that she had to try to cure her troubles, but was steadily getting worse. There was not one physician in the world who could bring in healing. She came near to God’s glorious Son, the power of Christ came into her, and the weakness in her went out; she became one who could go in peace (see Luke 8). Let us glory in the greatness of Jesus! He was here as the One who had the answer in Himself to every need of every man and He would draw near to us today as the One who has the answer to every need of every one of our hearts. There are needs and sorrows and problems with us that no one knows except Jesus, and He is here today to give His own touch of healing and make us understand afresh that He loves us, and His love is so great that He went into death for us. Can every one of us say, ‘Jesus loved me and gave Himself for me’? That is what held the apostle Paul steady through a life of pressure. He could speak of Jesus as “The Son of God, who has loved me and given himself for me”, Galatians 2: 20. It is the love of God in a Man that keeps us steady. The wind may come and the storms may blow, but let us remember that every storm blew upon the head of Jesus.

No one has gone through such suffering as Jesus our Saviour went through. There was never a cry from the lips of any man like that which went up from the lips of Jesus, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?”, Mark 15: 34. What a cry that was in those hours of darkness! Mark, as the recovered servant, tells us that the darkness was from the sixth hour until the ninth hour. For three hours from the third hour to the sixth hour the glorious perfection of Jesus shone out for the universe to see; it was the glory of the gathering up of the burnt-offering and the oblation. From the sixth hour to the ninth hour there was darkness. The very sun was darkened in the heavens. There was darkness over the whole land. No human eye could penetrate the darkness when God had to do with Jesus about our sins and sin itself. Jesus was there as in absolute accord with God as to the judgment of our sins. He was the One in whom sin was not and yet for your sake and mine He was made sin itself. The righteous God had to forsake Him as He hung there in darkness on the tree. But the ninth hour came, in which, with the dignity of the Victor, Jesus said, “It is finished”. Men took account of Him as crucified in weakness, but He lives by God’s power.

The cross stands as the eternal witness of the love of God, but the righteousness of God meant that Jesus, had to die and He went into all the darkness of the tomb. He was for three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. But on the third day the glory of the Father shone; the power of the love of the Father penetrated into the tomb. He wrought by His mighty power in Christ and selected that one Man from among the dead. God knows how many millions there were in death at that time. Jesus came out in all His personal glory and greatness, the light of the morning. The sun rose in the heavens, but the Son of God rose from among the dead. There were those who went to the tomb to embalm Him, as if He were still dead. As they were reaching the place they wondered about the great stone across the door of the tomb of Jesus—an impossible barrier for them. What a difficulty! Have you a difficulty, dear friend? When those beloved women looked, they saw that the stone had been rolled away. If we are with God, we find He removes difficulties. The Father, by raising Jesus from the dead, has shown that nothing is impossible for God. Christ is shining today as the glorious light of the morning. He is able to bring light and joy and power into every one of our lives.

He would tell us first that the forgiveness of sins is available for us. Can every one of us today say, ‘My sins are forgiven’? Can we turn to Jesus and bless Him as the One who died for our sins? If we do not know our sins are forgiven, what darkness there is! Oh do not remain in the dark! The prophet Jeremiah speaks of those who “stumble upon the mountains of twilight”, Jeremiah 13: 16. What a description of men in this world! Oh do not let us be here as persons that stumble, but as those upon whom the Sun of righteousness has arisen with healing in His wings. He is going to rise as the glorious Sun to bring light to the whole world before long. But now Jesus the Saviour is shining into the hearts of men, women, and children. He is bringing in the light that God is just waiting to bless us. He is looking for persons who will be here as those who trust Him and who seek to walk in the light as God is in the light. The enemy will attack. Do not let us deceive ourselves as to that. Do we not all find that sometimes doubts come in? but the blood of the Lord Jesus is the answer to every doubt.

It is said that Martin Luther had a dream at the time when God was using him in an outstanding way to bring back to men the glorious truth that we can be justified by faith. He dreamt that the devil drew near to him with a great roll in his hand. He began to unroll it, and there was recorded, line after line, the misdeeds and sins of Martin Luther. Luther said, ‘Go on, unroll more’ and he went on unrolling metre after metre. When he came to the end Luther said, ‘Is there no more there?’. ‘No’. Then Luther said, ‘Well, take your pen and write at the bottom of the list, “The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from all sin”. Can every one of us say that today? The answer to every doubt is that the blood of Jesus has been shed for us. The answer to every problem of the day is that Jesus is living in the glory on high. He is shining; all the glory of God is in His face, and as we come to know Him we learn to know the Father. We learn that we can speak to the Father as our Father. We find that the Father is over everything. He has given all things into the hands of the Son, but the Father is gloriously supreme.

The Lord Jesus reminded us that the Father makes His sun to rise on evil and good. That is one of the great statements of the Lord Jesus as He was sitting on the mountain in Matthew 5. As we see the sun let us remember it is the Father’s sun. The sun will continue to rise, and if there are clouds at times—and clouds do come—the thing is to get into the sunshine and then we see the bow in the clouds. God has given His own word (Genesis 9: 11–13) that there will never be such a flood again, but when the clouds come there will always be the rainbow. When there are problems and clouds, the rainbow of the faithfulness of God always shines. We are not going.to see it fully whilst we are here. Though we are always getting fresh impressions of the faithfulness of God, we only see part of the rainbow. We shall have to wait till we are in heaven to see the complete circle of the rainbow around the throne (Revelation 4: 3); but let us remember now, when the clouds come, that the faithfulness of God is still shining.

Eternal life means that we live on the sunny side of the road. It is not that we are occupied with the clouds; there are clouds, but we rely on the faithfulness of God, and we keep ourselves restful in the shining of the love of Jesus. As we are kept in the path of faith, we never find ourselves in any circumstance where the personal sympathy of Jesus will not be available to us. He has been tempted in every way in which we can be tempted, sin apart. So Jesus is able to sympathise. He takes account of the tears and the sorrows, He knew what it was to weep Himself. One of the most glorious statements in the whole of Scripture occurs when John, that great lover of Jesus, records, “Jesus wept”, John 11: 35. But as He wept He had the power to bring in life. Let us understand that in every cloud Jesus is able to shine. He is able to save us completely and to deal with every matter that comes into our pathway. He in Himself is the morning without clouds—glorious assurance of the day to come when His glory is going to be seen by all; but today God presents Him to you and me as the One who can be to us the light of the morning.

So let us come to Jesus today. May we understand as never before what a price has been paid. We are not to think we are our own; we belong to the Master who has bought us at a tremendous price. May the Spirit give us a fresh experience of the glorious privilege open to us to be here available for the Master’s use in the very little while that remains until we hear the assembling shout of the Lord Jesus. Then the opportunity for service will be over, and the last opportunity to confess the name of Jesus as Lord will be gone. Are we all confessing Jesus when we can? What opportunities there are in the school, or the office, in the shop, and at the house door, to confess our Saviour as the Lord of lords and King of kings.

The time for confession is nearly gone, let us use it while it is here, until we see the glorious face of Jesus and are with Him for ever. May the Spirit help us to be with Him now, so that when the moment comes when we depart every one may hear the Lord Jesus say, “Well done, thou good bondman”, Luke 19: 17. Jesus is the greatest Servant there ever has been, glorious, holy perfect Servant, but the Spirit would help us to serve the Lord Jesus in that which He gives each one of us to do. May we be here as watching and doing, waiting for the Lord to come, when we shall be with Him for ever. May the Lord bless the word.
